LO 1-3 - Differential Diagnosis

Clinical sorting

Spinal nerve vs peripheral nerve vs articular vs myofascial upper-extremity pain

This section also covers the common neurovascular entrapments that can drive upper-extremity symptoms, especially thoracic outlet, median nerve, ulnar nerve, and radial nerve patterns.

Fast sorting rule

For any arm complaint, decide whether the pattern is root-level neurologic, named peripheral nerve, joint/tendon mechanical, or trigger-point/myofascial referral. The lecture repeatedly emphasized that shoulder and arm complaints can have more than one cause, so keep a real differential even after you find one positive test.

EtiologyHistory patternPhysical exam cluesCommon examplesWhat confirms or redirects
Spinal nerve / radiculopathyNeck pain or provocation, dermatomal paresthesia, pain radiating in a stripe, weakness in a myotome.Positive Spurling, reflex/sensation/myotome changes; C4-C6 can mimic shoulder pain and C8 can mimic ulnar neuropathy.C5/C6 presenting like rotator cuff or epicondylitis; C8 presenting like ulnar distribution symptoms.Full upper-extremity neuro exam; MRI cervical spine if progressive deficit, myelopathy, trauma/infection/cancer concern, or refractory severe symptoms.
Peripheral nerve entrapmentNamed nerve territory; often nocturnal symptoms; symptoms worsen with local compression or repetitive use.Tinel/compression at entrapment site, distribution-specific weakness/atrophy, two-point discrimination loss, positive Durkan/Phalen for CTS.Carpal tunnel, pronator teres syndrome, cubital tunnel, Guyon's canal, thoracic outlet, radial tunnel/PIN patterns.EMG/NCS is gold standard for CTS and ulnar neuropathy when severity, surgery, or diagnosis is uncertain.
Articular / tendon / ligamentMechanical pain with motion, trauma, clicking, locking, painful arc, joint-line or insertion tenderness.Localized TTP, painful ROM/end-feel, instability tests, deformity, swelling, crepitus, weakness with tendon testing.AC arthritis/separation, rotator cuff impingement/tear, adhesive capsulitis, labral tear, biceps tendonitis, epicondylitis, UCL thumb tear.X-ray for trauma/bony disease; MRI/MR arthrogram/US depending on structure and severity.
Myofascial referred painAching or paresthesia-like pain that does not obey a dermatome or single named nerve; often posture/repetitive strain related.Palpation of a trigger point reproduces the familiar distal symptoms; neuro exam and entrapment tests may be negative.Scalenes mimicking CTS, pec minor/major, serratus posterior superior/anterior, latissimus dorsi referral into hand/fingers.Clinical diagnosis; improved with MFR, counterstrain, stretching, ergonomic change, and home exercise when red flags are absent.
EntrapmentNerve / locationSigns and symptomsKey discriminator
Thoracic outlet syndromeBrachial plexus/subclavian vessels compressed near scalenes, first rib/clavicle, or pec minor.Neurogenic: arm paresthesia, heaviness, weakness, symptoms with overhead posture. Vascular: swelling, coolness, color change, pulse changes.OMM targets first rib, clavicle, thoracic inlet, scalenes, pec minor, and drainage only after serious vascular compromise is excluded.
Carpal tunnel syndromeMedian nerve under transverse carpal ligament.Nocturnal numbness/tingling in thumb, index, middle, radial half of ring finger; thenar weakness/atrophy in advanced cases.Durkan is highly useful; EMG/NCS before surgery or unclear cases.
Pronator teres syndromeMedian nerve under/through pronator teres.Median distribution symptoms plus proximal forearm pain; carpal tunnel tests may be negative.Symptoms reproduced by pressure/Tinel at pronator teres; treat pronator/flexor compartment and interosseous membrane.
Cubital tunnelUlnar nerve at elbow.Fourth/fifth digit paresthesia, medial elbow symptoms, nocturnal symptoms, intrinsic weakness in severe cases.Tinel at cubital tunnel; worsens with elbow flexion or valgus/instability mechanics.
Guyon's canalUlnar nerve at wrist.Ulnar hand/hypothenar symptoms, possible grip/intrinsic weakness.Tinel at Guyon's canal; distinguish from cubital tunnel and C8 radiculopathy.

Q: A patient has nocturnal numbness in the thumb, index, and middle finger, positive Durkan compression at the wrist, and no neck-provoked symptoms. What bucket is most likely?

Answer

Peripheral nerve entrapment: carpal tunnel syndrome affecting the median nerve.

LO 4-7 - Workup, Management, OMT Plan

Clinical management

Diagnostic testing, OMT indications, contraindications, and the five-model treatment plan

TestBest use in upper-extremity complaintsExamples from this block
X-rayFirst-line for trauma, suspected fracture/dislocation, bony arthritis, calcific tendonitis, and AC separation classification.Shoulder AP/axillary/scapular-Y; Zanca for AC joint; boxer fracture; gamekeeper thumb before stress testing; jersey/mallet avulsion; scaphoid suspicion after FOOSH.
CTComplex fracture, subtle intra-articular bone injury, surgical planning, or when x-ray is equivocal but bony pathology remains high risk.Comminuted hand/wrist fracture, complex elbow injury, occult carpal fracture when MRI is unavailable or bony detail is needed.
MRISoft tissue tear, tendon/labrum/capsule pathology, neurologic compression anatomy, or refractory pain after conservative care.Rotator cuff partial/full tear, adhesive capsulitis complications, UCL thumb rupture, occult fracture, severe ligament injury.
MR arthrogramLabrum and intra-articular pathology.SLAP/labral tear with clunk, clicking, popping, or throwing-athlete shoulder pain.
UltrasoundDynamic tendon assessment, extra-articular biceps tendon, guided injections, soft-tissue masses, examiner-dependent ligament/tendon evaluation.Biceps tendon in bicipital groove, US-guided AC injection, UCL thumb evaluation, tendon retraction in jersey finger.
EMG/NCSGold-standard functional test for entrapment neuropathy severity and surgical planning.CTS and ulnar neuropathy; helps distinguish local entrapment from proximal neurologic causes.
Labs / aspirationWhen inflammatory, infectious, crystal, endocrine, or systemic disease is suspected.Septic olecranon bursitis aspiration; diabetes/thyroid/rheum workup when adhesive capsulitis has no obvious driver.
OMT is indicated when...OMT is contraindicated or must be delayed when...
Stable somatic dysfunction contributes to pain, drainage restriction, repetitive strain, myofascial referral, mild nerve entrapment, or compensatory mechanics.There is lack of consent, acute fracture/dislocation, open wound, infection/septic bursitis, unstable ligament rupture, tendon avulsion needing urgent surgery, progressive motor loss/atrophy, major vascular compromise, or red-flag neurologic findings.
Peripheral nerve symptoms are mild/early and there is no progressive weakness: use gentle decompressive MFR/BLT/Still, drainage work, and ergonomics.Do not aggressively manipulate suspected scaphoid fracture, boxer fracture with rotation/open wound, gamekeeper grade 3 rupture, jersey finger, mallet avulsion involving large articular surface, or unreduced dislocation.
Five-model planUpper-extremity application
BiomechanicalRestore position and motion of first rib, clavicle, SC/AC/GH/scapulothoracic mechanics, elbow/radial head, wrist/carpals, and hand restrictions.
Respiratory-circulatoryImprove thoracic inlet drainage, venous/lymphatic return, edema movement, and space around neurovascular tunnels.
NeurologicDecrease nociceptive drive, reduce reflex hypertonicity/facilitation, decompress peripheral nerves, improve axoplasmic flow when safe.
Metabolic-energeticAddress diabetes, thyroid disease, obesity, pregnancy, RA, healing capacity, sleep, inflammation, and medication risks that affect CTS/adhesive capsulitis/tendinopathy.
Behavioral-biopsychosocialModify overhead activity, vibration tools, gripping, keyboard/mouse setup, throwing mechanics, sleep position, and PT/OT/home exercise adherence.

Q: What test is considered the gold standard before surgery for carpal tunnel or significant ulnar neuropathy?

Answer

EMG/NCS, demonstrating slowed conduction or latency across the involved nerve segment.

LO 8 - Upper Extremity Screening Rubric

Skills test workflow

Upper-extremity screening exam: rubric sequence and diagnosis

Rubric focus

The lab emphasized three communication points before touch: explain what you will do, why you are doing it, and what you hope to achieve; obtain consent, wash hands, then perform the complete upper-extremity screen and identify the most restricted somatic dysfunction.

  1. SC joint and shoulder girdle. Thumb in jugular notch/fingers over proximal clavicle. Arm forward/back should move clavicular head posterior/anterior; arm up/down should move it inferior/superior. Decide if restriction is articular or soft tissue.
  2. AC joint and glenohumeral motion. Evaluate internal/external rotation and shoulder horizontal adduction/abduction patterns while monitoring AC mechanics and shoulder soft tissues.
  3. Elbow. Test flexion/extension, then passive valgus/varus joint play with the wrist stabilized.
  4. Radial head. Palpate anterior/posterior radial head glide during pronation/supination and decide articular radial head vs pronator/supinator soft-tissue barrier.
  5. Wrist. Test flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation.
  6. Radiocarpal and carpal bones. Wiggle proximal row then distal row; look for the most restricted scaphoid/lunate/capitate/triquetrum/trapezium/trapezoid/hamate relationship.
  7. Hand and fingers. Stabilize carpals, glide metacarpals, then screen MCP/PIP/DIP phalanges, especially if arthritis, trauma, or focal pain is present.
  8. Name and treat. State the most restricted UE somatic dysfunction, pick a safe modality, communicate reasoning, use minimum effective force, maintain timing, and recheck.
Rubric lineWhat "good" looks like
Communication and consentUses lay terms, asks for consent, repeats consent for sensitive regions, checks comfort, and explains expected benefit.
Articular vs soft tissueDoes not merely say "restricted"; identifies whether the barrier is likely joint play, capsule/ligament, muscle/fascia, or mixed.
Most restricted diagnosisAfter screening bilaterally, names one greatest restriction with position/motion language and ties it to treatment choice.
Treatment rubricPrecise contacts, correct stepwise recipe, localized force direction, minimum force, appropriate timing, recheck, and tissue texture change.

Q: During radial head screening, what motion pair should you compare?

Answer

Anterior/posterior radial head glide during pronation and supination, while deciding if the barrier is articular or soft tissue.

LO 9-10A - Shoulder Complaints

Shoulder region

Thoracic outlet, AC joint, rotator cuff/SITS, impingement, biceps tendonitis, labral tear, and adhesive capsulitis

ConditionPathophysiology / presentationExam and testsManagement and OMT
Thoracic Outlet SyndromeNeurovascular compression near scalenes, first rib/clavicle, or pec minor. Paresthesias/heaviness with overhead positions; vascular cases can cause swelling, coolness, color/pulse changes.Neurovascular exam, posture/first rib/clavicle/scalene/pec minor assessment; consider vascular workup if pulse/color/swelling changes.Education/posture, PT, treat first rib/clavicle/thoracic inlet/scalenes/pec minor gently. Urgent referral for vascular compromise or progressive neurologic deficit.
AC Joint ArthritisCommon with shoulder pain; trauma/overhead use; can set up rotator cuff impingement. Clicking/popping and superior shoulder pain.AC palpation sensitive but nonspecific; cross-body adduction; Zanca view more accurate than standard AP.Activity modification, PT, OMT, NSAIDs; US-guided steroid injection if refractory. Treat clavicle/SC/AC/scapular mechanics.
AC Joint SeparationTraumatic shoulder injury from lateral shoulder impact or FOOSH/elbow fall; anterosuperior pain.Piano key sign, AC tenderness; x-rays AP/Zanca/scapular-Y; classify Rockwood I-VI; rule out neurovascular compromise.Low-grade injuries conservative; high-grade/posterior/inferior displacement or neurovascular issues -> ortho. Avoid aggressive OMT across unstable separation.
Rotator cuff impingement / tearCompression of SITS tendons/bursa under coracoacromial arch; painful arc 60-120 degrees; supraspinatus most common.Neer, Hawkins-Kennedy, empty can, lift-off, drop-arm; differentiate from C4-C5 radic with Spurling/neuro exam.X-ray first for bony/calcific disease; MRI for suspected tear; rest/ice/heat/activity modification/PT 6-8 weeks; ortho for tear/labrum. OMT for rib/clavicle/scapula/GH mechanics.
Biceps tendonitisAnterior shoulder ache from proximal biceps tendon, often under coracoacromial arch; commonly coexists with rotator cuff tear or SLAP lesion.Bicipital groove tenderness; popping/catching/locking suggests SLAP. US for extra-articular tendon, MRI for cuff/labrum.Rest, PT, activity modification, steroid injection in selected cases; surgical referral if labral or cuff tear. Treat GH/scapulothoracic/pec/rotator cuff mechanics.
Labral tear / SLAPThrowing athletes; painful shoulder with clicking/popping/clunk.Clunk test may rule in; MR arthrogram is imaging of choice.Conservative trial if mild; sports med/ortho if persistent mechanical symptoms.
Adhesive capsulitisProgressive painful restriction of active and passive GH ROM; risks: diabetes, thyroid disease, immobilization, female sex, Parkinson, stroke, impingement.Capsular pattern: external rotation most limited, then abduction, then flexion. Scapular substitution is a major clue.Often 1-3 years but PT/OMM can hasten recovery. Seven stages of Spencer is high-yield; steroid injection may help early pain.

Q: A patient has both active and passive shoulder ROM restriction, external rotation is most limited, and they hike the scapula early during abduction. What diagnosis?

Answer

Adhesive capsulitis. The capsular pattern and scapular substitution are key.

LO 9-10B - Elbow and Forearm

Elbow and forearm

Medial/lateral epicondylitis, cubital tunnel, radial head issues, nursemaid's elbow, and olecranon bursitis

ConditionPresentation / pathophysiologyEvaluationTreatment
Medial epicondylitisGolfer's elbow: flexor/pronator tendinopathy at medial epicondyle; pain may radiate down anterior forearm.Clinical diagnosis: TTP at insertion, pain with resisted wrist flexion/pronation. Rule out ligament instability, fracture, synovitis, radic.Activity modification, counterforce brace, cock-up wrist splint if severe/repetitive, PT, NSAIDs; PRP may help longer-term. OMT: flexor/pronator MFR, radial/ulnar/interosseous membrane work.
Lateral epicondylitisTennis elbow: extensor/supinator tendinopathy at lateral epicondyle; dominant arm common.TTP lateral epicondyle, pain with resisted wrist extension/supination. Differentiate from radial tunnel/PIN and cervical radic.Same conservative plan; OMT to extensor compartment, radial head mechanics, wrist/carpals.
Cubital tunnel syndromeUlnar nerve entrapment at elbow; 4th/5th digit and hypothenar paresthesia, nocturnal symptoms, intrinsic weakness/atrophy in severe cases.Tinel at cubital tunnel, elbow flexion provocation, EMG if severe/uncertain; distinguish Guyon's canal and C8 radic.Activity modification, avoid prolonged elbow flexion/pressure, splinting/PT/OT, OMT to elbow/forearm/first rib/clavicle/scalenes when safe; transposition if severe pain/motor damage.
Radial head dysfunctionAnterior radial head often tied to supination restriction; posterior radial head tied to pronation restriction.Palpate radial head glide during pronation/supination; compare articular vs soft tissue barrier.Radial head ME, BLT/MFR/articulatory options, and recheck pronation/supination.
Nursemaid's elbowRadial head subluxation from annular ligament in children 12-35 months after axial traction; arm held flexed/pronated, reluctant to move.Assess fracture risk, vasculolymphatic integrity, elbow stability; image if atypical trauma or fracture concern.Supination-flexion reduction; refer for >1 week dislocation, recurrent dislocations, or failed reductions.
Olecranon bursitisPosterior elbow swelling from trauma/overuse, gout/pseudogout/psoriatic arthritis, or infection.Two-thirds nonseptic; erythema suggests infection but fever absent in some. Aspiration is gold standard when septic/crystal concern.Noninfectious: rest, ice, NSAIDs, compression; aspiration/steroid sometimes. Septic: antibiotics, culture-directed care. Avoid OMT over infected bursa.

Q: Which muscle group is involved in medial epicondylitis and what movement tends to provoke it?

Answer

Wrist flexors and pronators; pain is provoked by resisted wrist flexion/pronation and palpation at the medial epicondyle.

Wrist and hand

CTS, pronator teres, De Quervain, gamekeeper thumb, boxer fracture, jersey finger, and mallet finger

ConditionPresentation / pathophysiologyWorkupManagement
Carpal Tunnel SyndromeMedian nerve compression under transverse carpal ligament; nocturnal paresthesia in thumb/index/middle/radial ring; thenar weakness/atrophy if advanced.Durkan, Phalen, Tinel; EMG/NCS gold standard, especially before surgery.12 weeks night cock-up splint, hand PT, steroid injection selected cases, OMT to carpal bones, flexor retinaculum, interosseous membrane, forearm, thoracic inlet. Surgery for severe/refractory or motor deficit.

De Quervain tenosynovitisStenosing tenosynovitis of first dorsal compartment: abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis; radial wrist/thumb pain with gripping/lifting.Finkelstein/Eichhoff pain over radial styloid; x-ray only if bony differential; US can evaluate tendons.Thumb spica splint, activity modification, NSAIDs, PT/OT, injection if persistent; OMT to wrist/thumb/carpals/forearm when no acute tear/fracture.

Surgery if >30% articular surface or unstable.

Q: A player cannot actively flex the DIP after grabbing another player's jersey. What injury and treatment?

Answer

Jersey finger, an FDP avulsion; it needs early surgical repair.

LO 11A - Shoulder/Rib/Clavicle Techniques

OMT atlas I

First rib, supine ribs, clavicle, scapulothoracic, glenohumeral BLT/BM, Spencer, and radial head ME

TechniqueDiagnosis/useRecipe
First Rib BLTFirst rib/thoracic outlet/TOS/rib-clavicle mechanics.Supine. Thumb on posterosuperior first rib, fingers at anterior first rib. Disengage posterior/anterior articulations, balance anterior-posterior/medial-lateral/superior-inferior, patient turns head opposite until T1 rotates away, then respiratory cooperation until release.
Supine Rib BLTRib dysfunction and thoracic-rib coupling.Finger at rib angle draws rib head anterolaterally to disengage. Other hand stabilizes/pulls spinous processes toward physician to rotate vertebra away. Use breathing and hold until correction.
Clavicle BLTSC/AC/clavicle dysfunction, TOS, shoulder girdle restrictions.Seated. Thumbs under medial and lateral clavicle. Patient slouches/leans forward onto thumbs while physician resists and carries shoulder posteriorly; opposite shoulder retracts; balance clavicle over costoclavicular ligament with inhalation/hold.
Scapulothoracic BLT/BMScapula-rib, serratus/subscap/pec/lat/scapular dyskinesis, shoulder pain.Thumbs enter axillary space between scapula and ribs as patient elevates then lowers shoulder onto contacts. Move scapula through protraction/retraction, abduction/adduction, elevation/depression, and add humeral/breath cooperation to find balance.
Glenohumeral Joint BLTGH capsule restriction, internal/external rotation dysfunction, adhesive capsulitis support.Grasp proximal humerus, gently disengage laterally, patient places hand on opposite shoulder and retracts to increase disengagement. Raise elbow for internal rotation dysfunction, depress elbow for external rotation dysfunction; hold until strain resolves.
Seven Stages of Spencer with MEAdhesive capsulitis/GH ROM restriction; board high-yield.Support shoulder, apply stages: extension, flexion, circumduction with compression, circumduction with traction, abduction/external rotation, abduction, internal rotation, abduction with traction. Add isometric ME against physician resistance for selected stages; repeat 3-5 times and recheck ROM.
Radial Head ME - anteriorAnterior radial head / supination barrier.Cup elbow and wrist. Bring forearm into pronation to restrictive barrier; patient supinates against resistance 3-5 seconds; relax; take up slack further into pronation. Repeat and recheck.
Radial Head ME - posteriorPosterior radial head / pronation barrier.Bring forearm into supination to restrictive barrier; patient pronates against resistance 3-5 seconds; relax; take up slack further into supination. Repeat and recheck.

Q: What is the universal rib BLT idea from lab?

Answer

Disengage the rib, stabilize it, rotate the attached vertebra away, then use respiratory cooperation to reseat the rib in balanced tension.

LO 11B - Forearm, Wrist, Carpal Tunnel, Counterstrain

OMT atlas II

Forearm MFR, interosseous membrane MFR, carpal tunnel MFR/Still/FPR, wrist BLT, carpal Still/FPR, and upper-extremity counterstrain

TechniqueUseRecipe
Forearm flexor/extensor MFRMedial/lateral epicondylitis, pronator teres syndrome, repetitive strain.Contact flexor or extensor compartment; test fascial ease/bind in multiple planes; engage direct/indirect barrier and hold until release. Add slow wrist/finger flexion-extension for active cooperation.
Forearm interosseous membrane MFRDeep forearm restriction, nerve/vascular proximity, pronation/supination dysfunction.Grasp radius and ulna as levers. Toggle anterior/posterior, superior/inferior, compression/distraction; hold direct or indirect barriers until release, moving distal to proximal.
Flexor retinaculum / Carpal Tunnel MFRCTS, wrist/flexor retinaculum restriction, venous/lymphatic congestion.Fingers posterior wrist, thenar eminences anterior over transverse carpal ligament; gently spread/open like a book, adding superior/inferior and compression/distraction vectors. Patient opens/closes fingers slowly.
Carpal Tunnel Still/FPRCarpal tunnel/carpal bone restriction when compression and ease are tolerated.Still recipe: find ease in carpal/soft tissue vectors, add compression, then move through toward barrier/opening. FPR option: add compression and position of ease briefly, then return to neutral and recheck.
Carpal Bone Still/FPRSpecific scaphoid/lunate/capitate/carpal restriction from screening.Monitor restricted carpal bone; use metacarpal/thumb/finger as lever. Place bone in ease, add compression through metacarpal, then move through corrective arc. FPR variation uses compression plus ease and short hold.
Wrist BLTGlobal wrist/carpal ligamentous imbalance.Interlace hands around wrist, gently compress, carry through flexion/extension and radial/ulnar deviation to balance. Patient spreads/extends fingers maximally then relaxes, or adds wrist circumduction while physician holds vectors.
Counterstrain - pectoralis minorAnterior chest/shoulder pain, rounded shoulder, pec minor/TOS contribution.Tender point inferior/medial to coracoid. Supine; physician stands opposite side. Move upper extremity diagonally across chest and apply inferomedial compression to enhance scapular protraction.
Counterstrain - radial head lateralLateral epicondyle/forearm pain with supination-pronation activity.Tender point lateral to radial head near supinator. Extend, supinate, and slightly abduct forearm until tenderness improves; hold 90 seconds, slow return.
Counterstrain - medial epicondyleMedial epicondyle/proximal pronator tenderness with radiating anterior forearm pain.Tender point proximal medial forearm at pronator teres attachment. Flex, pronate, and slightly adduct forearm until tenderness improves; hold 90 seconds, slow return.
Lab flexibility

The same forearm/carpal contacts can be used as MFR, BLT, Still, FPR, or articulatory treatment by changing the force: direct/indirect barriers for MFR, balanced midpoint for BLT, ease-compression-motion for Still, and compression plus ease for FPR.

Q: What is the basic Still recipe used for the carpal tunnel and carpal bones?

Answer

Ease, compression, motion: find ease, add compression, then carry through a corrective arc and recheck.

Case Integration

Putting it together

Case-based diagnosis and treatment planning

Case 1 - Shoulder pain with painful arc

Vignette: A 48-year-old has atraumatic shoulder pain from 60-120 degrees abduction, positive Neer/Hawkins, and no Spurling/neuro findings.

Answer: Rotator cuff impingement. X-ray if bony/acromial/calcific concern; PT/activity modification; OMT to clavicle, first rib, scapulothoracic, GH, thoracic spine/ribs. MRI if weakness/tear or refractory.

Case 2 - CTS mimic

Vignette: Median-distribution tingling but Durkan/Phalen/Tinel at wrist are negative; pronator compression reproduces symptoms.

Answer: Pronator teres syndrome. Treat flexor/pronator MFR, interosseous membrane, radial head/forearm mechanics, ergonomics, PT.

Case 3 - Trauma thumb

Vignette: Ski fall, thumb MCP pain, laxity without endpoint after x-ray rules out fracture.

Answer: Suspect grade 3 UCL rupture. MRI/hand surgery; do not manipulate unstable ligament.

Case 4 - Frozen shoulder

Vignette: Diabetic patient with months of shoulder pain then stiffness; passive and active ROM limited, ER worst.

Answer: Adhesive capsulitis. PT, Spencer with ME, GH/scapulothoracic/first rib/clavicle OMT; consider early steroid injection for pain.

Stem clueMost likely answer
Nocturnal thumb/index/middle paresthesia + positive DurkanCarpal tunnel syndrome; splint/PT/OMT, EMG for severe/surgical cases.
Fourth/fifth digit paresthesia + Tinel at elbowCubital tunnel syndrome; distinguish C8 and Guyon's canal.
DIP cannot flex after grabbing jerseyJersey finger; early surgical repair.
DIP cannot extend after ball impactMallet finger; extension splint unless large articular avulsion/unstable.
Five-year-old? no; toddler after traction refuses to move elbowNursemaid's elbow; supination-flexion reduction after fracture screen.

Q: What should you always do after any upper-extremity OMT technique in the skills-test context?

Answer

Recheck the exact motion/tissue texture you diagnosed and describe the tissue texture change or treatment effect.

Week 7 Upper Extremity - High-Yield One-Pager

Rapid review: buckets, tests, must-not-miss injuries, screening order, and OMT recipes.

Diagnose

Four pain buckets

  • Spinal: dermatome/myotome/reflex, Spurling.
  • Peripheral: named nerve, local Tinel/compression, EMG.
  • Articular/tendon: mechanical pain, focal TTP, imaging as needed.
  • Myofascial: trigger point reproduces non-dermatomal pain.

Entrapment map

  • CTS: median nerve, thumb/index/middle, nocturnal.
  • Pronator: median symptoms + forearm/proximal provocation.
  • Ulnar: 4th/5th digits, cubital tunnel or Guyon's.
  • TOS: scalenes/first rib/clavicle/pec minor.
Clinical must-knows

Shoulder

  • AC arthritis: cross-body adduction, Zanca view.
  • Impingement: painful arc 60-120, supraspinatus common.
  • Adhesive capsulitis: active + passive restriction; ER worst.
  • SLAP/labrum: click/clunk; MR arthrogram.

Hand injuries

  • Gamekeeper grade 3 -> surgery within 21 days.
  • Boxer fracture -> check rotation; ulnar gutter if stable.
  • Jersey -> cannot flex DIP; early surgery.
  • Mallet -> cannot extend DIP; splint if <30% articular avulsion.
Screen and treat

Screening order

Consent/wash -> SC -> AC/GH -> elbow flex/ext + varus/valgus -> radial head glide with pron/sup -> wrist flex/ext + radial/ulnar deviation -> carpal rows -> metacarpals/phalanges -> name worst dysfunction.

Technique cues

  • BLT ribs: disengage rib, rotate vertebra away, breathe.
  • Still: ease, compression, motion.
  • Spencer: adhesive capsulitis high-yield.
  • Forearm MFR: flexors/extensors/pronator/interosseous membrane.
  • CTS OMT: retinaculum/carpal tunnel, wrist/carpals, drainage.
